system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2127-01-05 10:21:00 to 2127-01-06 17:37:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, tracheostomy, and a history of recurrent infections was admitted with altered mental status and respiratory failure. He was found to have multifocal pneumonia due to Serratia and Proteus, requiring intubation and ventilator support, and a vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus urinary tract infection. He was treated with cefepime for pneumonia and linezolid for the UTI, with successful weaning from the ventilator. His altered mental status, attributed to toxic metabolic encephalopathy, resolved with treatment. The citalopram dose was temporarily reduced due to interaction risk with linezolid. He was discharged to extended care on day 7 to complete his antibiotic courses, with glycopyrrolate added to manage secretions.
problems: Pneumonia due to other Gram-negative bacteria
Acute and chronic respiratory failure with hypoxia
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus

EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with PICC placed at OSH// PICC location

IMPRESSION: 

In comparison with study ___, there is a right subclavian PICC line in
place that extends to the lower SVC.  Continued diffuse bilateral pulmonary
interstitial opacities with tracheostomy tube in place.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with G-J tube, transfer from ___ for clogged
J limb// exchange

COMPARISON:  Percutaneous GJ tube check ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ and Dr.
___ radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure and has
reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
25 mcg of fentanyl and 0 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of  during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse.
MEDICATIONS: None.
CONTRAST: 20 ml of Optiray
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 1 min, 14 mGy

PROCEDURE:  Low profile MIC gastrojejunostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

The existing tube was injected with contrast and showed opacification of the
gastric rugae and duodenum.  An Amplatz wire was introduced into the jejunum.
The existing feeding tube was then removed. An ___ F sheath 3.5 cm stomal
length 45 cm low profile MIC gastrojejunostomy catheter was advanced over the
wire into position.  The balloon was inflated with 8 cc of dilute contrast. 
The wire was then removed. Contrast was injected to confirm Catheter position
within the jejunum.

The catheter was then flushed. Sterile dressings were applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Appropriately positioned new 18 ___ low profile 3.5 cm stoma length MIC
gastrojejunostomy tube.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a gastrojejunostomy tube for a new 18 ___ low
profile 3.5 cm stoma length MIC gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to
use.

diagnoses.long_title: Surgical operation with formation of external stoma as the cause of abnormal reaction of the patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at the time of the procedure
Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase and lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]
Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis without obstruction
Personal history of traumatic brain injury

procedures.long_title: Change Feeding Device in Lower Intestinal Tract, External Approach
Introduction of Nutritional Substance into Upper GI, Via Natural or Artificial Opening

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your doctors here. You were transferred to us because your feeding tube got clogged. Can you tell me if you're having any pain or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have pain here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Points to abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for letting me know. I see you're on a trach collar and not running a ventilator now. That's good progress from your recent pneumonia. Any fever, cough, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Breathing okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your sputum cultures showed Proteus and Pseudomonas, but you’ve already completed a 10-day course of Unasyn for that. No blood infection. You’re past the worst of the pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube not working. Can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why you’re here. Your GJ tube clogged, and the team at the other hospital couldn’t unclog it. You haven’t been getting your feeds or medicines through it since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medicines? Like my HIV pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve been missing your Truvada, darunavir, and other meds. We’ll fix that once we replace the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put in a new tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional radiology is scheduled to replace it today. It’s a quick procedure under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation so you’ll be comfortable. They’ll use a wire to guide the new tube in. It usually goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure just finished. They successfully replaced your GJ tube with a new low-profile one. It’s ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition will start tube feeds slowly this afternoon. Once we confirm it’s working, we’ll restart your HIV meds and other oral medications through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your liver enzymes are a bit high—ALT and AST are elevated. We did an ultrasound, which showed gallstones, but no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gallstones? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The stones aren’t causing inflammation. The liver enzyme rise might be from your HIV meds or past infections. We’ll need your primary doctor to follow this up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. Just monitoring. We’ll make sure your PCP checks it in the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your feeds are going well. No leaks or discomfort. We’ve restarted your HIV medications—Truvada, darunavir, ritonavir—and your seizure medicine, levetiracetam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about missing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Staying on schedule with your HIV meds is important. Your viral load is undetectable, and your CD4 count is 168, so your treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the steroids I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were started on methylprednisolone because your morning cortisol was low—5.9. But since you’re stable and not in shock anymore, we’re stopping the steroids now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I felt jittery on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing remains stable on the trach collar. The chest X-ray shows your lungs are clear, though there are some chronic changes from past infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still need oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue needing oxygen through your trach at home. That hasn’t changed. But you’re off the ventilator and pressors, which is excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night well. Vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where am I going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To a skilled nursing facility—we’ll send the name. They can manage your trach, feeds, and medications, and help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I come back here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless needed. But you’ll follow up with your primary doctor soon, especially for the liver enzyme issue and gallstones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on levetiracetam twice daily. That hasn’t changed. As long as you keep taking it, your seizures should remain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Keep up with your feeds, meds, and trach care. We’ll send all instructions to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your new tube is intact, no redness. You’ve had regular bowel movements and no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeds feel normal. No pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll document everything for the nursing team. You’re cleared to transfer later this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. One last thing—your discharge summary says to use sodium bicarbonate if the tube clogs again, and keep using glycopyrrolate for secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. And call if you develop fever, belly pain, or trouble breathing. Otherwise, keep following up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and gastrostomy status was admitted after transfer for a clogged GJ tube. He had recently been treated for aspiration pneumonia with Unasyn and was weaned from mechanical ventilation and pressors prior to admission. The clogged feeding tube was successfully replaced via interventional radiology, allowing resumption of tube feeds and oral medications, including antiretroviral therapy. Mild transaminitis was noted with ultrasound showing gallstones but no cholecystitis; outpatient follow-up was recommended. He remained stable on trach collar with no respiratory deterioration. He was discharged to extended care with plans for ongoing monitoring of liver enzymes and continuation of chronic medications.
